Jollibee Foods Corporation (JFC) was incorporated on January 11, 1978. The Company's principal business is the development, operation and franchising of quick service restaurants (QSRs) under the trade names "Jollibee", "Chowking", "Greenwich", "Red Ribbon", "Yong He King", "Hong Zhuang Yuan", "Mang Inasal", "Highlands Coffee", "Smashburger", "The Coffee Bean & Tea Leaf", "Milksha", "Tim Ho Wan", "Tortazo", "Burger King", "Panda Express", "Yoshinoya", "Common Man Coffee Roasters", "Tiong Bahru Bakery" and "Compose Coffee".  The other activities of JFC include manufacturing and property leasing in support of the QSR systems and other business activities.

Aside from the subsidiaries that develop and operate the Company's QSR trade names, JFC wholly owns Freemont Foods Corporation, which owns and operates Jollibee stores in Visayas and Mindanao, and Grandworth Resources Corporation, a real estate company which owns or leases some of the properties used as store sites.

By the end of 2024, there were 1,279 Jollibee stores nationwide, of which 840 were franchised and 439 were Company-owned. On international operations, Jollibee had 480 stores, of which 122 were franchised and 358 were company-owned with specific locations as follows: 75 in the US, 28 in Canada, two in Italy, 12 in the United Kingdom, one in Spain, 60 in the Middle East, 21 in Brunei, 22 in Singapore, 20 in Malaysia, two in Guam, 20 in Hong Kong, four in Macau, and 213 in Vietnam.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

## Company: Jollibee Foods Corporation (JFC)
Sector: Industrial / Food, Beverage & Tobacco
Jollibee Foods Corporation (JFC) was incorporated on January 11, 1978. The Company's principal business is the development, operation and franchising of quick service restaurants (QSRs) under the trade names "Jollibee", "Chowking", "Greenwich", "Red Ribbon", "Yong He King", "Hong Zhuang Yuan", "Mang Inasal", "Highlands Coffee", "Smashburger", "The Coffee Bean & Tea Leaf", "Milksha", "Tim Ho Wan", "Tortazo", "Burger King", "Panda Express", "Yoshinoya", "Common Man Coffee Roasters", "Tiong Bahru Bakery" and "Compose Coffee".  The other activities of JFC include manufacturing and property leasing in support of the QSR systems and other business activities.

Aside from the subsidiaries that develop and operate the Company's QSR trade names, JFC wholly owns Freemont Foods Corporation, which owns and operates Jollibee stores in Visayas and Mindanao, and Grandworth Resources Corporation, a real estate company which owns or leases some of the properties used as store sites.

By the end of 2024, there were 1,279 Jollibee stores nationwide, of which 840 were franchised and 439 were Company-owned. On international operations, Jollibee had 480 stores, of which 122 were franchised and 358 were company-owned with specific locations as follows: 75 in the US, 28 in Canada, two in Italy, 12 in the United Kingdom, one in Spain, 60 in the Middle East, 21 in Brunei, 22 in Singapore, 20 in Malaysia, two in Guam, 20 in Hong Kong, four in Macau, and 213 in Vietnam.

storedThesis:
Jollibee Foods Corporation runs a portfolio of quick-service brands anchored by its namesake chain in the Philippines, plus a growing overseas stable — Smashburger, Coffee Bean & Tea Leaf, Highlands Coffee, Tim Ho Wan, Milksha, Compose, Panda Express franchise rights, and more. The core business — fried chicken, burgers, and casual dining across Southeast Asia and North America — is easy enough to understand: real estate-heavy restaurant operations, franchise royalties, and brand licensing. Complexity comes from the sheer number of concepts under one roof and now a live corporate restructuring: JFC is spinning off its international operations into a separately listed entity (JFCI) on the Hong Kong exchange, distributed pro-rata to existing shareholders. That's a meaningful structural change to underwrite, not just a burger chain thesis.

Moat is mixed. Domestically, Jollibee has a real moat — decades of brand loyalty in the Philippines, dense store network, and switching costs baked into consumer habit (Filipinos overseas seek it out specifically). That's a genuine consumer-brand moat, similar to McDonald's in its home market. Internationally, it's much weaker: Smashburger and Yong He King are actively shedding stores and converting to franchising because they never built the density or brand equity to compete profitably against entrenched local players. Highlands Coffee, Compose, and Milksha are growing fast (system-wide sales up 25-47%) but that's market-share capture in fragmented categories, not yet proof of a durable advantage — it's execution, which can erode as competitors respond.

Management is aggressively acquisitive and financially engineering the structure (HK spinoff, JFCI) rather than showing capital discipline. Gross interest-bearing debt sits around ₱93.2bn, consistent with the reported 1.70x debt/equity — high for a business with only 7.7% average ROIC. The 10-year ROIC of 7.7% against that leverage is the central red flag: management is buying growth (multiple foreign acquisitions since 2010: Smashburger, CBTL, Highlands, Tim Ho Wan) without compounding returns on capital, a classic Rule #1 warning sign that growth isn't creating owner value proportionally. The Q2 2026 international EBITDA decline (-0.4%) despite double-digit sales growth confirms that overseas expansion carries real transition costs and hasn't scaled into profit yet. The Vietnam Highlands Coffee stake sale to the local founder and the HK spinoff at least suggest management is willing to simplify the structure and let capital follow returns, which is a mild positive signal, but the jury's out until JFCI actually lists and its balance sheet/economics become visible.

Valuation is unattractive right now. At ₱145 against a Rule #1 sticker price of ₱224.40, the current price already sits 29.2% above the 50% margin-of-safety buy price of ₱112.20 — you're paying full freight, not buying at a discount. P/B of 2.4x for a levered, single-digit-ROIC business is rich; the 2.4% dividend yield doesn't compensate for the growth-without-returns problem. Watch the JFCI spinoff terms closely — if the international unit lists with cleaner economics and Jollibee Philippines retains the high-ROIC domestic core with less debt, the sum-of-parts could re-rate the stock favorably. Also watch whether Smashburger/Yong He King franchising conversions actually stop the bleeding, and whether ROIC trends up post-restructuring.

Bottom line: watch, not buy at ₱145. The domestic moat is real and management is at least addressing the low-ROIC international sprawl via the HK spinoff, but current price offers zero margin of safety and the 7.7% ROIC against 1.70x leverage says capital allocation hasn't matched the growth story. Revisit after the JFCI listing completes and post-spinoff financials clarify whether either entity trades meaningfully below its own sticker price — ideally near or below the ₱112 MOS level for the combined position.
